---
title: "Pluggable classification backends"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`xplus()` historically drove every pseudo-labeling iteration and the final
refit through `glmnet::cv.glmnet()`. The development version turns that
learner into a pluggable slot: any model that can fit weighted binary or
fractional targets and return probabilities can drive the PLUS loop, and the
elastic-net fit remains the default. This article describes the backend
contract, the built-in learners, and the evaluation benchmark.

## Built-in backends

Five backends ship with the package. Pass a name or a configured
constructor to the `backend` argument of `xplus()`:

| backend | learner | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `"glmnet"` | `glmnet::cv.glmnet()` | default; honors `alpha` and `cv_measure`, records the CV measure in `history` |
| `"ranger"` | `ranger::ranger()` | probability forest for binary targets, regression forest for soft pseudo-labels; OOB `fit_predict` |
| `"gam"` | `mgcv::gam()` | one smoothing spline per feature; `max_features` guards the dimension cost |
| `"xgboost"` | `xgboost::xgb.train()` | logistic/regression objectives by target; out-of-fold `fit_predict` |
| `"lightgbm"` | `lightgbm::lgb.train()` | fastest tree backend; out-of-fold `fit_predict` |

Constructors expose learner hyperparameters with parsnip-harmonized names,
e.g. `xplus_backend_ranger(trees = 1000, mtry = 4)` or
`xplus_backend_xgboost(trees = 200, learn_rate = 0.05)`. `ranger`, `mgcv`,
`xgboost`, and `lightgbm` are in `Suggests`, so install them to use those
backends. A sixth path wraps any `parsnip` model spec directly:

```r
library(parsnip)
backend <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  xplus_backend_parsnip()
fit <- xplus(x, y, backend = backend)
```

`xplus_backend_parsnip()` flips the spec's mode per fit — classification on
binary iterative targets, regression on the fractional final ones — maps
case weights to `hardhat` weight vectors, injects engine seeds so
`xplus(seed = ...)` stays reproducible, and reuses out-of-bag scores when
the engine stores them. Specs whose model lacks a regression mode fail with
a clear message at the final stage.

```{r builtin}
library(xplus)
sim <- simulate_pu_data(n = 400, p = 8, boundary = "nonlinear",
                        prevalence = 0.4, label_propensity = 0.5, seed = 11)
unl <- sim$y == 0

fit_glmnet <- xplus(sim$x, sim$y, backend = "glmnet", max_iter = 30, seed = 3)
fit_ranger <- xplus(sim$x, sim$y, backend = xplus_backend_ranger(trees = 300),
                    max_iter = 30, seed = 3)

data.frame(
  backend = c("glmnet", "ranger"),
  auc_unlabeled = c(auc(sim$z[unl], as.numeric(predict(fit_glmnet))[unl]),
                    auc(sim$z[unl], as.numeric(predict(fit_ranger))[unl])),
  cutoff = c(fit_glmnet$cutoff, fit_ranger$cutoff),
  n_iter = c(fit_glmnet$n_iter, fit_ranger$n_iter)
)
```

On a nonlinear boundary the elastic-net logistic fit collapses toward chance
while the forest tracks the radial structure; on linear boundaries the
ranking reverses, which is exactly why the learner is now a choice rather
than a constant.

## The backend contract

`xplus_backend()` defines the minimal estimator interface — fit weighted
`(x, y)` data, then predict probabilities — shared by caret `modelInfo`
entries, sklearn `fit`/`predict_proba` estimators, and mlr3 `Learner`s:

| field | signature | role |
|---|---|---|
| `fit` | `fit(x, y, foldid, weights)` | fit binary or fractional targets; attach `attr(model, "xplus_cv_measure")` to report `"deviance"` or `"auc"` in `history` |
| `predict` | `predict(model, newx)` | finite probabilities in `[0, 1]` per row |
| `importance` | `importance(model)` | optional named feature scores for `get_importance()` |
| `fit_predict` | `fit_predict(model, x)` | optional honest predictions on the fitted rows (see below) |
| `uses_cv`, `parameters` | — | metadata: CV usage and tunable parameters (caret `modelInfo` style), the latter reserved for a future tuning bridge |

```{r custom}
constant <- xplus_backend(
  name = "constant",
  fit = function(x, y, foldid, weights) stats::weighted.mean(y, weights),
  predict = function(model, newx) rep(model, nrow(newx))
)
fit <- xplus(sim$x, sim$y, backend = constant, max_iter = 3)
fit$backend$name
```

## Honest training predictions

A subtlety of the contract: `xplus()` stores training predictions in
`object$pred_y` and calibrates the classification cutoff as the `qq`
quantile of positive predictions. High-capacity learners memorize their own
training targets, so in-sample scores for labeled positives sit far above
anything reachable — with a forest, the cutoff landed above every unlabeled
score and F1 collapsed to zero.

Backends may therefore declare `fit_predict(model, x)`: honest estimates on
the rows they were fitted on, in the same order. The ranger backend supplies
out-of-bag predictions; rows never out-of-bag fall back to `predict`. The
iterative pseudo-label fits deliberately keep plain `predict`, since the
self-training update relies on in-sample scores, but the stored predictions
and cutoff are honest — and `predict(fit)` without `newx` returns those
stored scores for non-glmnet backends, so training-data evaluation matches
what the model produces on unseen data.

## Benchmark

`inst/benchmarks/backends/compare_backends.R` fits every backend on
`simulate_pu_data()` boundaries (linear, interaction, nonlinear) and scores
predictions against the hidden labels, overall and inside the unlabeled
pool:

```sh
Rscript inst/benchmarks/backends/compare_backends.R [outdir] [reps] [quick]
```

Representative results (3 replicates, n = 1000, p = 12, prevalence 0.4,
label propensity 0.5):

| backend | boundary | AUC (unlabeled) | F1 (unlabeled) | seconds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| glmnet | linear | 0.96 | 0.79 | 0.4 |
| ranger | linear | 0.92 | 0.68 | 2.0 |
| gam | linear | 0.95 | 0.79 | 22.0 |
| xgboost | linear | 0.85 | 0.59 | 3.0 |
| lightgbm | linear | 0.91 | 0.67 | 2.9 |
| glmnet | interaction | 0.72 | 0.48 | 0.4 |
| ranger | interaction | 0.74 | 0.48 | 2.1 |
| gam | interaction | 0.66 | 0.47 | 163.0 |
| xgboost | interaction | 0.72 | 0.47 | 2.8 |
| lightgbm | interaction | 0.74 | 0.49 | 2.9 |
| glmnet | nonlinear | 0.50 | 0.27 | 0.5 |
| ranger | nonlinear | 0.91 | 0.69 | 2.2 |
| gam | nonlinear | 0.93 | 0.77 | 23.9 |
| xgboost | nonlinear | 0.83 | 0.55 | 1.3 |
| lightgbm | nonlinear | 0.89 | 0.65 | 0.9 |

ranger is competitive on every boundary and roughly ten times faster than
gam, lightgbm is the fastest learner after glmnet, and glmnet remains the
cheapest option while still winning cleanly on linear structure. The
boosting backends work out of the box but their default hyperparameters are
untuned — the nonlinear AUC gap versus gam is exactly what a tuning pass
should close.

The honest cutoff transfers to held-out data: ranger reaches test-set F1 of
0.76–0.80 with the same stored cutoff, which the memorized in-sample
calibration could not.

## Model selection without negatives

`xplus_grid()` fits every candidate on shared bootstrap seeds and ranks
them by `pu_score()` — the positive-vs-unlabeled AUC of the honest stored
predictions, which orders learners consistently under SCAR labeling:

```r
xplus_grid(x, y, c("glmnet", "ranger", "lightgbm"))
xplus_grid(x, y, xplus_backend_xgboost,
           params = expand.grid(trees = c(100, 300), learn_rate = c(0.05, 0.15)))
```

On the `lacsSample` dataset (600 curated PU text documents reduced to a
300-term TF-IDF matrix, 153 positives vs 447 unlabeled) the PU ranking
recovers the expected text-model ordering — glmnet 0.999 > ranger 0.966 >
lightgbm 0.958 > xgboost 0.938 — and ranks xgboost hyperparameter settings
correctly (300 trees at `learn_rate` 0.05 beat the smaller, faster
settings). Linear learners win on sparse text; forests win on curved
boundaries. The leaderboard makes that choice an empirical one.

## What is next

The `parameters` field already declares tunable hyperparameters in caret
`modelInfo` form (`trees`, `mtry`, `min_n` for ranger; `trees`, `learn_rate`,
`tree_depth` for the boosting backends; `alpha` for glmnet; `k` for gam), and
`xplus_backend_parsnip()` already bridges the tidymodels engine zoo. The
remaining seam is learner selection: ranking backends and tuning their
parameters needs evaluation metrics that stay honest without negative
labels — the problem the `fit_predict` hook was built for.
